title: Soul's Beauty
text:
Beneath the arch of Life, where love and death,

terror and mystery, guard their sanctuary,

I saw Beauty on a throne,

and though her eyes are abandonment,

I drew her in the simplicity of my breath.

Hers is the gaze-above and below

the heaven that curves over you-

by sea or sky or woman, there is only one law:

to be the servant of her palm and crown.


This is what the Lady of Beauty knows,

in whose praise your voice and hand stir,

long wisdom in the flight of your hair,

the daily beating in your heart and feet,

with what irremediable passion, in how many flights!

How many forms and ways her days possess!




"Soul's Beauty"
editorial_note: The translation follows the supplied Spanish Rossetti text while preserving the English source title.

title: For the Mary Magdalenes
editorial_note: The translation keeps the plea for mercy and preserves the source's unusual 'quails or koalas' image.

title: Restlessness
text:
No, do not come near! I want from far away

to love you and desire your two eyes.

For happiness is beautiful only while one waits,

while there remains a glimmer of hope.


No, do not come near! More tender are

sweet restlessness, waiting, and fear.

Everything is lovelier insofar as it is sought

and anticipated by intuition.


No, do not come near! Why this, and what for?

Only from far away does everything shine with starry brilliance;

admiration makes sense only at a distance.

No, let your two eyes not come near me!
editorial_note: The translation keeps distance as the condition that preserves desire, hope, and admiration.

title: Shipbuilders Build You White Ships...
text:
Shipbuilders build you white ships,

falconers raise falcons for you,

bees bring you a honeycomb from the sun,

fishermen fish gold from the sand,

peasants harvest fruits in the fields,

hunters gather deer antlers,

monks copy the gospels for you,

painters present their icons and frescoes,

blacksmiths forge the monastery doors,

juniper trees pour incense into the thuribles,

thujas forge golden censers for you,

but I beg you

only for the acorn

that lies beneath the forest branches,

for a child hungry for joy

when he finds it in winter.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the contrast between royal offerings and the humble winter acorn for a hungry child.
